To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The anatomical/physiological model based registration method was able to generate more accurate deformable registration than the image based method for the prostate and bladder.

the deformable registration method using the anatomical/physiological model can provide more accurate dose calculation than the image-based deformable registration method in terms of the DVH parameters of target volume and organs at risk (OARs).

(1) the anatomical/physiological model based registration method is more accurate than the image based method in terms of both the mean distance between corresponding structures and the mean distance between points within a structure, and (2) the anatomical model based registration method can be used to improve the accuracy of the image based method.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new method of image registration that is based on a deformable anatomical/ physiological model of the body and that is capable of handling the non-rigid deformations that can occur in the body due to respiration and organ motion.
the use of the finite element method (FEM) to model deformations of biological tissues and organs.
the development of new image-based and model-based deformable registration techniques for medical imaging, and with their evaluation and clinical validation in radiation oncology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
deformable image registration is a valuable and important component of image guided radiotherapy, but that the current state of the art is not yet sufficient for widespread clinical adoption.

the use of deformable registration methods for the purpose of radiotherapy dose recalculation in the context of anatomical/physiological change is a promising technique, but that there is a long way to go before it is ready for clinical use.

the use of deformable registration methods in radiotherapy has been proven to be beneficial and that the use of such methods should be considered in all radiotherapy treatment planning scenarios where the target and/or organs at risk move.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed a method for predicting radiation dose in the presence of organ motion.

we have developed an anatomical/physiological based deformable registration method that can be applied to a variety of imaging modalities, and that we have compared the accuracy of the deformable registration to a commercial image based method.
we have developed and tested a new deformable registration method for image-guided adaptive radiation therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the deformable registration methods are not as good as the rigid registration method for dose calculations in the head and neck.
the use of deformable registration methods in radiotherapy planning is feasible and that there is no clear winner among the three different methods we evaluated.
there is no single method of deformable image registration that is optimal for all situations.
